A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LongDocURL benchmark. Their main text, tables, figures, scoring procedures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations, input-paradigm ablations, and qualitative case studies on LongDocURL, including appendix results.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds human-baseline results and an analysis of sampled GPT-4o errors.

M1.justification: The document-processing, QA-generation, and automated/human-verification pipeline remains unchanged. Section 5's suggestions for layout-aware training and staged reasoning are future directions, not implemented method components.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 396 English documents, 2,325 QA pairs, eight document types, and 20 subtasks. The new human evaluation and error audit use subsets of existing coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds a Human Experts comparator in Tables 3 and 7, evaluated on 102 sampled questions. Existing model comparator sets remain unchanged, including the LLaVA-Next-Interleave-DPO entries already present in v1's Table 7.

E3.justification: V3 adds human evaluation on 102 uniformly distributed samples and a random audit of 97 GPT-4o errors. The existing 30-page cut-off, merging ablation, answer extraction, and scoring protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's two qualitative case studies, v3 adds a systematic GPT-4o failure analysis in Section 5 and Appendix G: 97 sampled errors, a seven-category distribution, and examples illustrating distinct failure mechanisms. Existing input ablations and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added human scores and error-category percentages are point estimates without a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantive human-reference and diagnostic findings: an overall human score of 84.8 on 102 questions, and error proportions including 32.7% perceptual, 20.6% inconsistent-format, and 10.3% extractor errors. Existing model scores remain unchanged. The human subset does not establish a matched-sample performance gap against the full-benchmark model scores.

T1.justification: The scoring definitions and list-matching pseudocode in Appendix D.5 are unchanged. Neither version introduces new theoretical results, proofs, or formal assumptions.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about the benchmark, semi-automated construction pipeline, 20 subtasks, and evaluation across 26 configurations.

C2.justification: Section 5 and Appendix G add important qualifications concerning formatting-sensitive scoring and answer-extractor failures. They also attribute model differences to multimodal training and DPO, and discuss layout-aware training and staged reasoning. These substantially expand interpretation beyond v1's aggregate comparisons and two cases.

D1.justification: The prompts, input-selection and merging pseudocode, hardware, temperature setting, annotation staffing, and advertised code/data link are retained. The new studies do not add corresponding implementation instructions or detailed human-evaluation procedures.

R1.justification: Section 2, the cited works, and the benchmark's positioning relative to prior document-understanding research remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section ordering are retained. V3 inserts Section 5 and Appendix G, makes small language and affiliation edits, adds acknowledgments, and removes the Ethical Impact section.

P2.justification: V3 adds a substantial visual error-analysis presentation: the distribution chart and example in Figures 6–7, plus six appendix examples in Figures 16–21. Tables 3 and 7 gain human-baseline rows. Earlier figures are retained and renumbered, with conference-footer and pagination changes.

improvement.justification: The systematic error audit strengthens interpretation by distinguishing model failures from scoring and extraction failures, while the human baseline supplies a useful reference absent from v1. These gains are limited by unchanged scoring problems and sparse human-study documentation, including the absence of matched-subset model results.
